documents.title: Chat GPT & AI Support (sample syllabus statements)
documents.summary: Teaching-center page that explains ChatGPT's limits and gives faculty three sample syllabus statements (no use, limited use, full use) from OSU plus statements from other universities. It asks instructors to state their position in the syllabus and Canvas and lists assignment-design tactics.
documents.stance_why: The page says "Faculty may wish to allow students to use generative AI tools, provide specific parameters for its use, or prohibit its use" and offers three tiers of sample statements, so it sets no stance itself and hands the decision to instructors.

units.why: The sentence lists three options for faculty ("allow", "provide specific parameters", "prohibit"), so the page sets no single rule and leaves the choice to each instructor; P04 fits because the decision is per instructor.
units.anchor: provide specific parameters for its use, or prohibit its use
units.policy: Faculty may allow generative AI, provide specific parameters for its use, or prohibit its use for course assignments and assessments.

units.why: Sample statements are grouped under headings by how much AI is allowed ("Do NOT Allow", "in Some Circumstances", "Full Use"), a three-level scheme, so P05 (named tiers) fits better than P110 which covers only the supply of templates.
units.anchor: For Faculty Who Allow Full Use of Generative AI Tools in the Learning Environment
units.frag_start: For Faculty Who Allow Full Use
units.policy: Sample syllabus statements are sorted into three tiers: no generative AI allowed, use in some circumstances or with explicit permission, and full use.
units.fit_note: The anchor is the third of three tier headings.

units.why: The page says "Sample statements from OSU and other higher education institutions that can be included in course syllabi", so ITLE supplies ready-made syllabus language; this is P110 (templates) rather than P09 because it supplies, not requires, a statement.
units.anchor: statements from OSU and other higher education institutions that can be included in course syllabi
units.policy: ITLE provides sample statements from OSU and other institutions that can be included in course syllabi.

units.why: "It is important that faculty clearly communicate to students the acceptable use of generative AI" tells instructors to state their expectations; P09 fits (state AI expectations to students).
units.anchor: faculty clearly communicate to students the acceptable use of generative AI
units.frag_end: use of generative AI in their course(s).
units.policy: Faculty clearly communicate to students the acceptable use of generative AI in their course(s).

units.why: "Such communication should be included via a statement in the syllabus and/or Canvas course site in addition to verbally communicating" names the channels for the rule, an instruction to instructors; P09 fits and the channels are the content.
units.anchor: should be included via a statement in the syllabus and/or Canvas course site
units.policy: The communication of the AI position is included in a statement in the syllabus and/or Canvas course site, in addition to verbally communicating the faculty's position in class.

units.why: "it should not be used to replace or undermine students' original work and effort" is a limiting principle on AI use stated for all; P32 fits because AI must not replace the student's own effort.
units.anchor: it should not be used to replace or undermine students' original work and effort
units.policy: Generative AI should not be used to replace or undermine students' original work and effort.

units.why: "can be a useful tool for learning and education" names a benefit of AI without making it a rule, which is P87 (benefits) not P44 (career skill).
units.anchor: generative AI can be a useful tool for learning and education
units.policy: Generative AI can be a useful tool for learning and education.

units.why: The sample statement says "Students are prohibited from using any generative AI tools ... when completing course assignments", a flat ban on assignments; P01 (prohibit by default on graded work).
units.anchor: Students are prohibited from using any generative AI tools
units.policy: Students are prohibited from using any generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Bing AI, or Bard when completing course assignments.

units.why: "will be considered plagiarism" classifies the banned use as misconduct, so P36; the penalty is coded separately as P37.
units.anchor: will be considered plagiarism
units.frag_start: Use of these tools, or other
units.policy: Use of these generative AI tools will be considered plagiarism.

units.why: "could result in the student failing the course" is a concrete stated penalty, P37.
units.anchor: could result in the student failing the course
units.frag_start: Use of these tools, or other
units.policy: Use of the banned tools could result in the student failing the course.

units.why: "Any incident detected will be addressed through the university's academic integrity procedures" routes cases into the formal process; P81 fits (formal procedure), though it does not give steps.
units.anchor: Any incident detected will be addressed through the university's academic integrity procedures
units.policy: Any incident detected will be addressed through the university's academic integrity procedures.
units.fit_note: Only names the process, with no steps, forms or deadlines.

units.why: In the OSU limited-use sample, "Students may access and use generative AI tools ... to assist them in their learning of the course content" permits learning use; P12 fits (understanding the content), not graded answers.
units.anchor: Students may access and use generative AI tools
units.policy: Students may access and use generative AI tools, such as ChatGPT, Bing AI, or Bard, to assist them in their learning of the course content.

units.why: "generating ideas for writing assignments" is listed as an appropriate use, so P15 (brainstorming).
units.anchor: generating ideas for writing assignments
units.policy: Appropriate uses may include generating ideas for writing assignments.

units.why: "checking facts of a phenomenon" is an appropriate use that helps understanding, nearest P12 (tutor-like use) though it is fact-checking.
units.anchor: checking facts of a phenomenon
units.policy: Appropriate uses may include checking facts of a phenomenon.
units.fit_note: Fact-checking a phenomenon is not exactly explaining concepts.

units.why: "assessing a paper for grammatical errors that are written by the student" permits AI to check the student's own writing, P91 (editing and proofreading).
units.anchor: assessing a paper for grammatical errors that are written by the student
units.policy: Appropriate uses may include assessing a paper for grammatical errors that is written by the student.

units.why: "students are prohibited from using generative AI tools to completely produce, reproduce, and/or manufacture paper" bars AI from producing the submitted work, P19.
units.anchor: prohibited from using generative AI tools to completely produce, reproduce, and/or manufacture paper
units.policy: Students are prohibited from using generative AI tools to completely produce, reproduce, and/or manufacture paper and/or other assignments without using any personal effort devoted to the learning process.

units.why: "students should check to ensure they do not conflict with copyright laws or other's proprietary information" is a copyright and IP caution, P52.
units.anchor: check to ensure they do not conflict with copyright laws or other's proprietary information
units.policy: Before using generative AI tools, students should check to ensure they do not conflict with copyright laws or other's proprietary information.

units.why: The OSU full-use statement "Students may use generative AI tools ... to help them learn course content, complete course assignments" welcomes broad use by default, P02.
units.anchor: to help them learn course content, complete course assignments, or do other course-related tasks
units.frag_start: Students may use generative AI tools
units.policy: Students may use generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Bing AI, or Bard, to help them learn course content, complete course assignments, or do other course-related tasks.

units.why: "Students are expected to provide attribution for any text created using generative AI tools" requires acknowledgement of AI use, P24.
units.anchor: expected to provide attribution for any text created using generative AI tools
units.policy: Students are expected to provide attribution for any text created using generative AI tools as appropriate.

units.why: This is a quoted Texas Tech template, not OSU policy: "AI-generated submissions are not permitted and will be treated as plagiarism" bans AI-produced work, P19.
units.anchor: AI-generated submissions are not permitted and will be treated as plagiarism
units.policy: In the quoted Texas Tech sample, AI-generated submissions are not permitted and will be treated as plagiarism.

units.why: Quoted Texas Tech template: "Developing strong competencies in this area will prepare you for a competitive workplace" gives careers as the reason to do the writing yourself, P94.
units.anchor: Developing strong competencies in this area will prepare you for a competitive workplace
units.policy: In the quoted Texas Tech sample, developing strong writing competencies without AI prepares students for a competitive workplace.

units.why: Quoted University of Iowa template: using "artificial intelligence affordances like ChatGPT" to write a substantive portion is "violations of academic integrity", P19 for the ban on having AI do the writing.
units.anchor: has another person/entity do the writing of any substantive portion
units.frag_start: the following would be considered violations
units.policy: In the quoted Iowa sample, having another person or entity, including AI such as ChatGPT, do the writing of any substantive portion of an assignment is an academic integrity violation.

units.why: Quoted Colorado template: "no more than 25% of the student work should be generated by AI" is a numeric cap on AI-generated work, P16.
units.anchor: no more than 25% of the student work should be generated by AI
units.frag_start: In such cases, no more than
units.policy: In the quoted Colorado sample, no more than 25% of the student work should be generated by AI.
units.fit_note: Concerns generated content (text, video, audio, images) in general, not only code.

units.why: Quoted Colorado template: "Any student work submitted using AI tools should clearly indicate what work is the student's work and what part is generated by the AI" marks AI parts in the submission, P24.
units.anchor: what work is the student's work and what part is generated by the AI
units.frag_start: Any student work submitted using AI
units.policy: In the quoted Colorado sample, student work submitted using AI tools should clearly indicate which part is the student's and which part is AI-generated.

units.why: Quoted Colorado template: "please reach out to me for a conversation before submitting your work" tells students to ask when unsure, P10.
units.anchor: reach out to me for a conversation before submitting your work
units.frag_start: If any part of this is
units.policy: In the quoted Colorado sample, students who find any part confusing or uncertain should reach out to the instructor for a conversation before submitting work.

units.why: Quoted Minnesota template: AI "may be used for [assignment types A, B & C] with appropriate citation, but not for [assignment types D, E & F]" sets per-assignment permission with citation, P04 (assignment-level rule).
units.anchor: may be used for [assignment types A, B & C] with appropriate citation
units.policy: In the quoted Minnesota sample, AI language models may be used for some assignment types with appropriate citation, but not for others.
units.fit_note: Also requires citation for the permitted assignment types.

units.why: Quoted Minnesota template: "You are responsible for fact checking statements composed by AI language models" makes students verify output, P31.
units.anchor: You are responsible for fact checking statements composed by AI language models
units.policy: In the quoted Minnesota sample, students are responsible for fact checking statements composed by AI language models.

units.why: Quoted UMass Amherst template: "I expect you to clearly attribute what text was generated by the AI tool" requires attribution inside the work, P27 as it marks the AI text where it appears (colored font, quotes, parenthetical).
units.anchor: clearly attribute what text was generated by the AI tool
units.frag_start: When you submit your assignment, I
units.policy: In the quoted UMass Amherst sample, students clearly attribute which text was generated by the AI tool, for example in a different colored font, direct quotation, or an in-text parenthetical citation.

units.why: Quoted Iowa full-use template: "students must cite any AI-generated material that informed their work" requires citation, P24.
units.anchor: students must cite any AI-generated material that informed their work
units.frag_start: To be consistent with our scholarly
units.policy: In the quoted Iowa sample, students must cite any AI-generated material that informed their work and use quotation marks or other appropriate indicators of quoted material when appropriate.

units.why: Quoted Iowa full-use template: "Students should indicate how AI tools informed their process and the final product" asks for a description of process, P26 (reflection on AI use); "how you validated any AI-generated citations" is a detail the type does not cover.
units.anchor: Students should indicate how AI tools informed their process and the final product
units.frag_start: Students should indicate how AI tools
units.frag_end: transparency about their use in your work.
units.policy: In the quoted Iowa sample, students indicate how AI tools informed their process and the final product, including how they validated any AI-generated citations.
units.fit_note: A written description of AI's role and citation validation, not a full transcript or log.

units.why: "Discuss value and relevance of assignments as they relate to skill development" asks instructors to explain to students why assignments matter, P66.
units.anchor: Discuss value and relevance of assignments as they relate to skill development
units.policy: Instructors discuss the value and relevance of assignments as they relate to skill development.

units.why: "Require students to incorporate in-class discussions, experiences, experiments, demonstrations" is an assignment redesign that makes AI use harder, P35.
units.anchor: Require students to incorporate in-class discussions, experiences, experiments, demonstrations
units.policy: Instructors require students to incorporate in-class discussions, experiences, experiments, demonstrations, etc. in writing assignments, online discussions, and other text-based assignments.

units.why: "Focus assignments and assessments on higher-order thinking skills" redesigns assessment around analysis and creation, P35.
units.anchor: Focus assignments and assessments on higher-order thinking skills
units.policy: Instructors focus assignments and assessments on higher-order thinking skills, having students analyze, critique, evaluate, and create.

units.why: "Require specific sources, time ranges, and extensive use citations" is an assignment design tactic against AI, P35.
units.anchor: Require specific sources, time ranges, and extensive use citations
units.policy: Instructors require specific sources, time ranges, and extensive use of citations.

units.why: "Have students complete smaller assignments in class" moves work into supervised, in-class settings, P33.
units.anchor: Have students complete smaller assignments in class.
units.policy: Instructors have students complete smaller assignments in class.

units.why: "Require students to submit subcomponents of assignment for review and evaluation" is a staged-submission redesign, P35.
units.anchor: Require students to submit subcomponents of assignment for review and evaluation
units.policy: Instructors require students to submit subcomponents of an assignment for review and evaluation.

units.why: "Have students use Tracking Changes ... and turn in both a marked up version and a clean version" has students hand in drafts as process evidence, P26.
units.anchor: turn in both a marked up version and a clean version
units.policy: Instructors have students use Tracking Changes while working on assignments and turn in both a marked up version and a clean version.
units.fit_note: Submitted by students as process evidence, not as an AI-use disclosure.

units.why: "Consider authentic assessments" suggests redesigning assessment in response to AI, P35.
units.anchor: Consider authentic assessments.
units.policy: Instructors consider authentic assessments.

units.why: "Sometimes ChatGPT will produce responses that are factually incorrect or biased, and cite non-existent or incorrectly labeled sources" warns that output is unreliable, P31.
units.anchor: factually incorrect or biased, and cite non-existent or incorrectly labeled sources
units.policy: ChatGPT sometimes produces responses that are factually incorrect or biased, and cites non-existent or incorrectly labeled sources.

units.why: "it is difficult for faculty to discern if students have cheated" states a limit on verification, P82.
units.anchor: it is difficult for faculty to discern if students have cheated or been unethical
units.policy: It is difficult for faculty to discern if students have cheated or been unethical in the work they submit.

units.why: Output "not flagged when run through a plagiarism detector such as Turn It In" says detectors miss AI text, so detectors are not dependable, P39 (fit is partial since it speaks of plagiarism checkers).
units.anchor: not flagged when run through a plagiarism detector such as Turn It In
units.policy: ChatGPT text with citations is not flagged when run through a plagiarism detector such as Turn It In.
units.fit_note: Says a plagiarism detector misses ChatGPT text; it does not say not to use detectors.

units.why: "This page will continue to be updated as we learn more" says the guidance is provisional, P54.
units.anchor: This page will continue to be updated as we learn more
units.policy: This page will continue to be updated as ITLE learns more about how best to support faculty on campus.

units.why: "ITLE will be working to develop additional resources and helping support faculty" commits the center to support faculty with AI, P63.
units.anchor: ITLE will be working to develop additional resources and helping support faculty
units.policy: ITLE will be working to develop additional resources and helping support faculty and instructors regarding ChatGPT and other generative AI software.

units.why: "Contact us if you need additional support or resources" offers consultation with ITLE for AI questions, P63.
units.anchor: Contact us if you need additional support or resources
units.policy: Faculty can contact ITLE for additional support or resources relating to the use of ChatGPT and other AI software.

units.why: "Visit our Student AI Support page for more resources to share in your classroom" directs instructors to a further page, P115.
units.anchor: Visit our Student AI Support page for more resources to share in your classroom!
units.policy: Instructors can visit the Student AI Support page for more resources to share in their classroom.

documents.title: AI Misuse Guidelines for Instructors
documents.summary: ITLE guidance for instructors on handling suspected AI misuse: talk privately and with positive intent, do not rely on inaccurate detectors, ask for a supervised redo or oral exam, and report confirmed cases per University Policy. It sets no rule on whether AI is allowed.
documents.stance_why: The page governs response to misuse ("If instructors suspect students have violated academic integrity policies by misusing AI") and never sets whether AI is allowed; it only says to consider updating assignment guidelines "to prohibit AI use" if misuse recurs, so the allowed use is left to instructors.

units.why: "address the issue promptly through education-focused conversations with the students" prescribes how instructors respond to suspected AI misuse: educationally. P68 fits better than P57 because the emphasis is education over punishment.
units.anchor: address the issue promptly through education-focused conversations with the students
units.frag_start: they should address the issue promptly
units.policy: Instructors who suspect AI misuse should address the issue promptly through education-focused conversations with the students.

units.why: "Having a conversation in person with the assumption of positive intent can set a collaborative tone until a violation is proven" presumes good faith, P68.
units.anchor: the assumption of positive intent can set a collaborative tone until a violation is proven
units.frag_start: Having a conversation in person with
units.policy: Instructors have an in-person conversation assuming positive intent, setting a collaborative tone until a violation is proven.

units.why: "listen openly to students' processes and reasoning" with "another faculty or TA in the meeting" is talking to the student and gathering context before escalating, P57.
units.anchor: explain questionable areas of submitted work, and listen openly to students' processes and reasoning
units.frag_start: In a private discussion with another
units.policy: In a private discussion with another faculty or TA present, the instructor discusses concerns with the student, explains questionable areas of submitted work, and listens openly to the student's processes and reasoning.

units.why: "requiring students to redo assignments under supervision could provide clarity" uses a supervised redo as a check of the student's ability, P34.
units.anchor: requiring students to redo assignments under supervision could provide clarity
units.policy: If suspicions remain after discussion, requiring students to redo assignments under supervision could provide clarity.
units.fit_note: Supervised redo of the assignment; oral exam is given as an example elsewhere.

units.why: "focus on using integrity violations as learning opportunities while fairly enforcing established academic conduct guidelines" pairs educative response with enforcement, P68.
units.anchor: using integrity violations as learning opportunities while fairly enforcing established academic conduct guidelines
units.policy: Instructors should focus on using integrity violations as learning opportunities while fairly enforcing established academic conduct guidelines.

units.why: "a transparent conversation grounded in positive assumptions, can prevent confrontations and promote ethical scholarship" justifies the approach proactively; P68 since it frames the response as preventive and educative.
units.anchor: a transparent conversation grounded in positive assumptions, can prevent confrontations
units.frag_start: Approaching the situation proactively, with a
units.policy: Approaching a suspected violation proactively with a transparent conversation grounded in positive assumptions can prevent confrontations and promote ethical scholarship.

units.why: "AI detectors have been found to be inaccurate for AI misuse" tells instructors detectors are unreliable, P39.
units.anchor: AI detectors have been found to be inaccurate for AI misuse
units.policy: AI detectors have been found to be inaccurate for AI misuse.

units.why: "Consult with other professors or TAs for their opinion" and "insight into the student's typical writing style" gather context from colleagues before escalating; nearest P57 (context before escalating), though P57 is about talking with the student.
units.anchor: Consult with other professors or TAs for their opinion
units.frag_start: Consult with other professors or TAs
units.policy: Instructors consult with other professors or TAs for their opinion on whether the assignment submission appears suspicious; they may have insight into the student's typical writing style and capabilities.
units.fit_note: Gathering colleague opinion, not talking with the student; the use of typical writing style as evidence is not covered.

units.why: "Don't accuse but explain the specific areas that seem unusual and ask the student to explain their process" is talking with the student first, P57.
units.anchor: Don't accuse but explain the specific areas that seem unusual
units.policy: Instructors speak with the student privately, do not accuse, explain the specific areas that seem unusual, and ask the student to explain their process and reasoning.

units.why: "request the student redo the assignment in a monitored setting, such as taking an oral exam" checks understanding by oral exam, P34.
units.anchor: redo the assignment in a monitored setting, such as taking an oral exam
units.policy: If suspicion remains after discussing it with the student, the instructor requests that the student redo the assignment in a monitored setting, such as taking an oral exam on the material.

units.why: "Make the academic integrity policies clear to the student regarding the consequences of AI misuse, such as failing the assignment or course" asks instructors to state penalties; P37 fits because failing the assignment or course is named.
units.anchor: consequences of AI misuse, such as failing the assignment or course
units.frag_start: Make the academic integrity policies clear
units.policy: Instructors make the academic integrity policies clear to the student regarding the consequences of AI misuse, such as failing the assignment or course, and focus on it as a learning opportunity.

units.why: "If AI misuse is confirmed, enforce the academic integrity policies accordingly" treats confirmed misuse as an integrity case, P36.
units.anchor: If AI misuse is confirmed, enforce the academic integrity policies accordingly.
units.policy: If AI misuse is confirmed, instructors enforce the academic integrity policies accordingly.

units.why: "Report any infractions to the proper channels per University Policy" is the formal reporting step, P81.
units.anchor: Report any infractions to the proper channels per University Policy.
units.policy: Instructors report any infractions to the proper channels per University Policy.

units.why: "Consider updating assignment guidelines and policies to prohibit AI use if it is a recurring issue more explicitly" advises tightening the course rule after repeated misuse; nearest P35 (redesigning around AI), though it is a policy revision.
units.anchor: Consider updating assignment guidelines and policies to prohibit AI use
units.policy: Instructors consider updating assignment guidelines and policies to prohibit AI use more explicitly if misuse is a recurring issue.
units.fit_note: A revision of the course AI rule toward prohibition after recurring misuse, not an assignment redesign.

units.why: "Explain limitations to students" asks instructors to give students the reasons and limits of the AI rules, P66.
units.anchor: Explain limitations to students.
units.policy: Instructors explain limitations to students.

units.why: The page links "AI Misuse Decision Pathway Document" and "Question Guide for Suspected Academic Misconduct", pointing to further guidance, P115.
units.anchor: AI Misuse Decision Pathway Document
units.frag_start: View Official Document and References List
units.policy: The page links an official document and references list, an AI Misuse Decision Pathway Document, and a Question Guide for Suspected Academic Misconduct.

documents.title: Student Artificial Intelligence Support: Leveraging AI Tools Responsibly
documents.summary: Student-facing strategies from ITLE for using AI tools responsibly: check the syllabus, disclose and cite, verify output, and use AI for explanation, brainstorming, proofreading, practice problems and summaries without replacing own thinking. The page says it was drafted by ChatGPT and edited by staff.
documents.stance_why: The strategies "should only be used after verifying with the instructor that using AI-generated content on learning assignments is permissible" and tell students to "read the syllabus", so the page defers the decision to instructors while describing permitted uses; delegates.

units.why: The page says AI tools "can be valuable resources for university students, assisting with research, writing, and learning", a benefit statement, P87.
units.anchor: can be valuable resources for university students, assisting with research, writing, and learning
units.policy: AI tools can be valuable resources for university students, assisting with research, writing, and learning.

units.why: "it is crucial to utilize these tools ethically and responsibly" is a general call with no specific content, P116.
units.anchor: it is crucial to utilize these tools ethically and responsibly
units.policy: It is crucial to utilize AI tools ethically and responsibly.

units.why: "should only be used after verifying with the instructor that using AI-generated content on learning assignments is permissible" makes the instructor the gatekeeper and has students check first, P10.
units.anchor: verifying with the instructor that using AI-generated content on learning assignments is permissible
units.policy: The student strategies should only be used after verifying with the instructor that using AI-generated content on learning assignments is permissible.
units.fit_note: Also frames the instructor as gatekeeper for AI on learning assignments.

units.why: "Carefully read the syllabus and verify the permissible use of AI usage first" tells students to learn the course rules; P78 not P10 because the first step is reading the syllabus, not asking.
units.anchor: Carefully read the syllabus and verify the permissible use of AI usage first.
units.policy: Students carefully read the syllabus and verify the permissible use of AI first.

units.why: "Some instructors may not allow AI-generated content in assignments, or they may have specific rules" says rules vary by instructor, P04.
units.anchor: Some instructors may not allow AI-generated content in assignments
units.policy: Some instructors may not allow AI-generated content in assignments, or they may have specific rules about how it is used.

units.why: "Inform instructors of AI tool use and explain how they were used" requires disclosure to the instructor, P24.
units.anchor: Inform instructors of AI tool use and explain how they were used.
units.policy: Students inform instructors of AI tool use and explain how they were used.

units.why: "Just like any other source, AI-generated content should be cited" asks for citation; P24 chosen over P45 because the rule is about citation, not collaboration.
units.anchor: AI-generated content should be cited.
units.policy: Just like any other source, AI-generated content should be cited.

units.why: "AI tools are meant to assist and enhance learning, not replace critical thinking and originality" keeps the student as the thinker, P32.
units.anchor: AI tools are meant to assist and enhance learning, not replace critical thinking and originality
units.frag_start: It is important to remember that
units.policy: AI tools are meant to assist and enhance learning, not replace critical thinking and originality in academic work.

units.why: "use ChatGPT to seek further explanations on complex topics or ask for specific examples" is the tutor use, P12.
units.anchor: use ChatGPT to seek further explanations on complex topics
units.policy: A student may use ChatGPT to seek further explanations on complex topics or ask for specific examples to solidify understanding.

units.why: "Claude 2 can provide suggestions, offer code snippets, or explain different approaches" for a programming problem; P16 (AI-generated code) fits partly, as no conditions on the snippets are given.
units.anchor: Claude 2 can provide suggestions, offer code snippets, or explain different approaches
units.frag_start: In cases where a student encounters
units.policy: For a difficult programming problem, a student can use Claude 2 for suggestions, code snippets, or explanations of different approaches.
units.fit_note: Code snippets are offered as help with no cap or citation condition; the page elsewhere warns against shortcuts.

units.why: "Students should avoid using AI tools as shortcuts or substitutes for genuine effort and critical thinking" limits use to protect the student's own work, P32.
units.anchor: avoid using AI tools as shortcuts or substitutes for genuine effort and critical thinking
units.frag_start: Students should avoid using AI tools
units.policy: Students should avoid using AI tools as shortcuts or substitutes for genuine effort and critical thinking.

units.why: "view AI tools ... as collaborators" frames AI as a collaborator; P45 is the nearest type though no existing integrity rules are mentioned.
units.anchor: view AI tools, such as ChatGPT, Google Bard or Cluade 2, as collaborators
units.frag_start: Students can view AI tools, such
units.policy: Students can view AI tools, such as ChatGPT, Google Bard or Claude 2, as collaborators to enhance academic endeavors.
units.fit_note: Calls AI a collaborator without tying it to collaboration or citation rules.

units.why: "collaborate with Google Bard to brainstorm unique plotlines, explore different character arcs" is brainstorming with AI, P15.
units.anchor: collaborate with Google Bard to brainstorm unique plotlines
units.frag_start: a student working on a creative
units.frag_end: imaginative scenarios to inspire and enrich their writing.
units.policy: A student working on a creative writing assignment can collaborate with Google Bard to brainstorm plotlines, explore character arcs, or generate scenarios.

units.why: "it is crucial not to rely solely on AI-generated content without personal input, analysis, and evaluation" requires the student's own contribution, P32.
units.anchor: not to rely solely on AI-generated content without personal input, analysis, and evaluation
units.frag_start: Although collaborating with AI tools can
units.policy: It is crucial not to rely solely on AI-generated content without personal input, analysis, and evaluation.

units.why: "should always verify the information through reputable sources and cross-referencing" tells students to check AI output, P31.
units.anchor: should always verify the information through reputable sources and cross-referencing
units.frag_start: Users who employ AI tools to
units.policy: Users who employ AI tools to generate initial ideas or insights should always verify the information through reputable sources and cross-referencing.

units.why: "students should avoid treating AI-generated content as unquestionable truth" asks for critical evaluation of output, P31.
units.anchor: avoid treating AI-generated content as unquestionable truth
units.frag_start: Although AI tools can be helpful,
units.policy: Students should avoid treating AI-generated content as unquestionable truth and should evaluate its accuracy, credibility, and objectivity.

units.why: "AI tools should serve as catalysts for critical thinking rather than replacing students' cognitive engagement" is the thinker principle, P32.
units.anchor: AI tools should serve as catalysts for critical thinking rather than replacing students' cognitive engagement
units.frag_start: AI tools should serve as catalysts
units.policy: AI tools should serve as catalysts for critical thinking rather than replacing students' cognitive engagement.

units.why: "AI tools can be used advantageously for tasks like proofreading, grammar checks, and language suggestions" is a writing-support permission, P91.
units.anchor: tasks like proofreading, grammar checks, and language suggestions
units.frag_start: AI tools can be used advantageously
units.policy: AI tools can be used for tasks like proofreading, grammar checks, and language suggestions to improve the quality of written work.

units.why: "they should not be used for complex tasks that require subject knowledge, creativity, or originality" bars AI from generating the substantive work, P19.
units.anchor: should not be used for complex tasks that require subject knowledge, creativity, or originality
units.frag_start: Although AI tools can help with
units.policy: AI tools should not be used for complex tasks that require subject knowledge, creativity, or originality, and students should not simply rely on them to generate complex scientific formulas, solve intricate mathematical problems, or provide expert-level insights.
units.fit_note: Frames the limit by task complexity, not by whether the output is submitted.

units.why: "Students can request specific problem statements for various subjects, aiding in practice and comprehension" allows AI-made practice problems, P14.
units.anchor: Students can request specific problem statements for various subjects
units.policy: Students can request specific problem statements for various subjects, aiding in practice and comprehension.

units.why: "Relying solely on ChatGPT for problem-solving may hinder the development of problem-solving skills" is a skill-building rationale, P41.
units.anchor: may hinder the development of problem-solving skills that require personal analysis and critical thinking
units.policy: Relying solely on ChatGPT for problem-solving may hinder the development of problem-solving skills that require personal analysis and critical thinking.

units.why: "Students should actively analyze the problems, devise strategies, and work through the solutions independently" keeps the student as problem-solver, P32.
units.anchor: actively analyze the problems, devise strategies, and work through the solutions independently
units.frag_start: Students should actively analyze the problems,
units.policy: Students should actively analyze the problems, devise strategies, and work through the solutions independently to develop their problem-solving abilities.

units.why: "assist in outlining key ideas from papers, generating quotes, and providing summaries for annotated bibliographies" permits AI to digest literature; P104 fits (screening and annotating sources) though it also covers summaries.
units.anchor: assist in outlining key ideas from papers, generating quotes, and providing summaries for annotated bibliographies
units.frag_start: AI tools such as Google Bard can
units.policy: AI tools such as Google Bard can assist in outlining key ideas from papers, generating quotes, and providing summaries for annotated bibliographies.

units.why: "Students should read and critically think about the papers and use Bard or Claude 2's output to supplement their understanding" conditions the permission on the student doing the reading, P32.
units.anchor: Students should read and critically think about the papers
units.policy: Students should read and critically think about the papers and use the AI tool's output to supplement their understanding.

units.why: "AI tools can help students identify potential unintentional plagiarism by highlighting similarities between their work and existing sources" lets students check their own work, P125.
units.anchor: identify potential unintentional plagiarism by highlighting similarities between their work and existing sources
units.policy: AI tools can help students identify potential unintentional plagiarism by highlighting similarities between their work and existing sources.

units.why: "AI tools can guide formatting citations and references according to specific academic styles" is a permitted use no type names (citation formatting), so UNCOVERED rather than stretching P91.
units.anchor: AI tools can guide formatting citations and references according to specific academic styles
units.frag_start: Citation and Referencing Support: AI tools
units.policy: AI tools can guide formatting citations and references according to specific academic styles such as APA and MLA.
units.uncovered_note: Allows AI to help format citations and references.

units.why: "They also should verify the accuracy of generated citations" warns that AI citations may be wrong, P31.
units.anchor: verify the accuracy of generated citations
units.frag_start: They also should verify the accuracy
units.policy: Students should verify the accuracy of generated citations and adhere to the guidelines of their educational institution.

units.why: "Students should be cautious about using AI tools to generate content with proper attribution or to plagiarize others' work" warns about plagiarism via AI; closest is P120 (unintentional plagiarism).
units.anchor: be cautious about using AI tools to generate content with proper attribution or to plagiarize
units.frag_start: Students should be cautious about using
units.policy: Students should be cautious about using AI tools to generate content with proper attribution or to plagiarize others' work.
units.fit_note: Warns generally about plagiarism by AI, without saying AI reproduces sources.

units.why: "select tools that prioritize ethical practices, such as protecting user data, ensuring transparency, and respecting user privacy" tells students to choose tools by ethics criteria, P117.
units.anchor: select tools that prioritize ethical practices, such as protecting user data
units.policy: Students who elect to use AI as a learning support should select tools that prioritize ethical practices, such as protecting user data, ensuring transparency, and respecting user privacy.

units.why: "Ethical AI tools prioritize data security and implement measures to protect user information" is a data-protection criterion for choosing tools, P50.
units.anchor: Ethical AI tools prioritize data security and implement measures to protect user information
units.frag_start: Data Protection: Ethical AI tools prioritize
units.policy: Ethical AI tools prioritize data security and implement measures to protect user information from unauthorized access or misuse.
units.fit_note: A criterion for tool choice, not an instruction to protect one's own data.

units.why: "Transparency: ... making users aware of the underlying algorithms, limitations, and potential biases" names bias as a tool-choice criterion, P53.
units.anchor: making users aware of the underlying algorithms, limitations, and potential biases
units.policy: Ethical AI tools provide transparency in their operations, making users aware of the underlying algorithms, limitations, and potential biases.
units.fit_note: Bias appears as a transparency criterion for choosing tools.

units.why: "This page was written by ChatGPT (GTP-3.5) ... edited from its original version by Alysia Ropp" discloses AI-made course material and human editing, P48.
units.anchor: This page was written by ChatGPT (GTP-3.5)
units.frag_end: edited from its original version by Alysia Ropp.
units.policy: The page was written by ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) after being given information about responsible AI use for students, and was edited from its original version by Alysia Ropp.
units.fit_note: Discloses AI authorship and human editing; does not say materials are reviewed as a rule.

notes: Coder B. Document 1 includes quoted sample statements from other institutions (Texas Tech, Iowa, Colorado, Minnesota, UMass Amherst) coded as templates, not as OSU policy. Where a unit's type fit only partly a fit_note is given; one UNCOVERED unit (AI for formatting citations).
